new_statements.quote: En proto-Nord-Centre-Vanuatu (PNCV), l'accent était paroxytonique, et c'était encore sans doute le cas en proto-Torres-Banks (PTB). En mwerlap, comme on va le voir plus en détail ci-dessous, les voyelles finales du PTB se sont amuïes. L'accent tombe majoritairement sur la syllabe finale, mais il n'est pas complètement fixe (il peut donc moins facilement servir d'outil diagnostique que dans d'autres langues pour déterminer si un morphème est enclitique ou suffixal, par exemple). Il s'agit d'un accent de longueur et d'intensité, mais la différence entre syllabes toniques et atones est relativement peu marquée, ce qui donne une intonation relativement « plate ».
new_statements.translation: In Proto-North-Central Vanuatu (PNCV) the accent was paroxytone [penultimate], and this was doubtless still the case in Proto-Torres-Banks (PTB). In Mwerlap, as we will see in more detail below, the PTB final vowels were lost. The accent falls predominantly on the final syllable, but it is not completely fixed (so it is less usable than in other languages as a diagnostic for deciding whether a morpheme is an enclitic or a suffix, for example). It is an accent of length and intensity, but the difference between stressed and unstressed syllables is relatively weakly marked, which gives a relatively 'flat' intonation.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted from the saved OpenEdition HTML; HTML meta confirms citation_firstpage 157, citation_lastpage 221, publication date 2023/07/01, doi 10.4000/1232y, title 'Éléments de description du mwerlap (langue du Nord-Vanuatu)', author Agnès Henri). The quoted passage is at line 200, section '2.1.1. Accent tonique', OpenEdition paragraph 22, exactly as quoted; the only differences are the inline footnote callouts '(PNCV 6)' and 'paroxytonique 7' (footnotes 6 = PNCV forms from Clark 2009, 7 = Clark 2009:16) which the reader dropped. Para. 114 (line 2308) also confirmed verbatim: 'Les formes indépendantes sont toniques, l'accent portant sur la dernière syllabe, comme dans l'ensemble des…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is on the last syllable of the word in the large majority of words (an oxytone system that arose historically from Proto-Oceanic penultimate stress after the posttonic final vowels were lost); the author cautions that the placement is not entirely fixed, and that stress (realised by length and intensity) is phonetically weak. Independent pronouns are likewise stressed on the last syllable 'like all stressed words of the language' (para. 114). François 2005: 451 gives the same final-stress rule as an areal generalisation over the 17 Torres-Banks languages including Mwerlap.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not stated synchronically. Historically, François 2005 (sec. 3.1, 5.1) and Henri 2023 (para. 33) assume Proto-Torres-Banks had primary penultimate stress with secondary stress on every second syllable leftward; Henri notes the pretonic (word-initial) vowel does not always delete.
new_statements.exceptions: Henri: 'il n'est pas complètement fixe' (not completely fixed), without listing the exceptions; sec. 1.3.1 para. 11 notes that the three Mere Lava dialect zones (Tesmet, Aota, the other three villages) differ phonetically in intonation and accentuation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('mots accentués de la langue'); data from Henri's own 2013 and 2015 fieldwork with speakers of all five Mere Lava villages plus Gaua, Santo, Efate and Maewo communities (sec. 1.4.1). Statement is descriptive-impressionistic, no instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: Henri 2023 describes Mwerlap of Mere Lava (five villages) with speakers also from Merig-descended and Gaua/Santo/Efate/Maewo diaspora communities; this is the language-level node merl1237 (ISO mrm; Codrington's 'Merlav', Tryon's Merlav/Merig lists). Henri notes three intra-island dialect zones (Tesmet, Aota, the rest) that differ in intonation and accentuation, so 'not completely fixed' may partly reflect dialect variation.

readall_conflicts: Lynch 2000 says nothing about Mwerlap; its claim that the Banks language Mwotlap has regular penultimate stress (p.59, p.77, after Crowley TOL) is contradicted for the whole Torres-Banks area by Francois 2005:451 ("words are now systematically stressed on their final rather than their penultimate syllable (contra Lynch 2000:77)") and, for Mwerlap specifically, by Henri 2023 sec. 2.1.1 para. 22 (accent predominantly on the final syllable, not completely fixed; length-and-intensity accent with a weak tonic/atonic contrast; Table 1 mmerir with initial stress as an instance of the caveat). The existing catalog record (fixed final, unreviewed) stands on Henri 2023 + Francois 2005; Lynch 2000 neither supports nor contradicts it because it does not describe the language.
